summary: This is a theoretical "field synthesis" paper by Garrick Holmes (RIFOR) proposing that intrinsic hydrogen bond asymmetry in water molecules (Gunkel et al., 2024) and the hydration solid framework (Harrellson et al., 2023) together govern the structure and electrical properties of the DNA hydration shell. The paper is entirely conceptual/hypothesis-generating (TRL 1), proposing four experiments to test the mechanism but reporting no original experimental data. It connects published findings across biophysics, structural biology, and electrochemistry to argue that the DNA minor groove functions as a hydration solid and that its asymmetric water shell contributes to DNA's electrical conductance pathway.

content_blocks.title: Abstract
content_blocks.content: The paper proposes that two independently established experimental findings intersect in the DNA hydration shell: (1) hygroscopic biological materials are 'hydration solids' governed by the hydration force in nanoscale pores (Harrellson et al., 2023); (2) water molecules are intrinsically asymmetric hydrogen-bond donors with one strong and one weak bond, anti-correlated and refreshed on sub-picosecond timescales (Gunkel et al., 2024). The paper proposes the DNA hydration shell is a hydration solid, that molecular bond asymmetry determines ordering and exchange dynamics of first-shell water, and that the asymmetric shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway. Four experiments are proposed using existing methods. No original experimental data is presented.

content_blocks.title: Section 1: On Field Synthesis
content_blocks.content: Defines 'field synthesis' as the practice of identifying published results across disciplines, recognizing structural connections, and proposing integrated research pathways for evaluation by domain experts. The paper explicitly positions itself as a conceptual synthesis exercise, not an experimental report.

content_blocks.title: Section 2: The Hydrated Helix — Background Evidence
content_blocks.content: Summarizes established findings on DNA hydration: (1) DNA requires water to maintain B-form; dehydration causes conformational change. (2) High-resolution crystallography resolves an ordered 'spine of hydration' in the minor groove. (3) Chiral SFG spectroscopy shows DNA confers handedness on first-shell water, constituting a structured phase distinct from bulk solvent (McDermott et al., 2017; Perets and Yan, 2017; Perets et al., 2024). (4) Drug binding disrupts chiral water structure (Santiago et al., 2025). (5) NMR shows spine water in the minor groove resides ~1 ns at 4°C and 10–15 ns at lowest temperatures measured, ~10x longer than major groove water (Halle and Denisov, 1998). All evidence cited is from published literature; no new data presented.

content_blocks.title: Section 3: The Hydration Solid Framework
content_blocks.content: Describes Harrellson et al. (2023) framework: hygroscopic biological materials (bacterial spores, pollens, fungal walls) exhibit convergent mechanical behavior governed by the hydration force — a short-range repulsive interfacial force dominating transport and elasticity at nanometer-scale pore dimensions. In spore cortex (~4 nm pores), overlapping hydration force fields retard water transport by orders of magnitude beyond conventional prediction. The paper's first proposal: the DNA minor groove (a nanometric channel bounded by sugar-phosphate backbones with anionic phosphate oxygens and base-edge heteroatoms) satisfies the geometric requirements of a hydration solid. This is a conceptual extension of published work, not a new experiment.

content_blocks.title: Section 4: The Asymmetric Molecule and Proposed Mechanism
content_blocks.content: Describes Gunkel et al. (2024): ultrafast spectroscopy of isotopically dilute water shows the two H-bonds donated by a single water molecule are markedly anti-correlated in strength (one strong, one weak), refreshed in <500 femtoseconds. Measurement was made in dimethylformamide; not yet tested in pure water. Minor-groove spine water resides ~1 ns at 4°C — ~3 orders of magnitude longer than the anti-correlation refresh — so asymmetry is a standing property during each residence event. Proposed mechanism: in the minor groove, a water molecule donates to chemically inequivalent acceptors (strong anionic phosphate oxygens vs. weaker base-edge heteroatoms). Under the anti-correlation rule, matched strong-to-strong / weak-to-weak bonding biases stable occupation of hydration positions (ordering consequence). Mismatched molecules require re-randomization of the anti-correlation to rearrange, adding an exchange barrier beyond conventional translational/rotational models (exchange consequence). All mechanistic content is theoretical.

content_blocks.title: Section 5: The Electrical Hydrogen Bond
content_blocks.content: Summarizes published evidence that hydrogen bonds are electrical structures: (1) Compton X-ray scattering on ice shows substantial covalent character with electron sharing (Isaacs et al., 1999). (2) Correlated vibrational spectroscopy in liquid water shows charge movement through the H-bond network: hydroxide ions donate ~8% more negative charge, hydronium ions accept ~4% less (Flór et al., 2024). (3) Femtosecond spectroscopy (Bakker group, AMOLF): proton shuttles between neighboring oxygens in <100 fs; ≥15 water molecules participate in moving one proton's charge; proton transfer between acid and base runs through H-bonded water wire of 2–4 molecules. (4) DNA charge transport: charge travels through 100 bp (34 nm) DNA; a single mismatched base pair cuts signal by ~half (ratio 2.3 ± 0.4, Slinker et al., 2011). (5) DNA conductance: 414 bp DNA between gold electrodes measured ~10 TΩ at 30% RH and ~250 MΩ at 80–90% RH — a ~40,000-fold drop reversible on drying (Tuukkanen et al., 2005). Paper proposes the asymmetric hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway; damage altering the groove alters the shell and thus the pathway.

content_blocks.title: Section 6: Proposed Experiments
content_blocks.content:
Four experiments proposed, all using existing methods, none yet performed:

6.1 Isotopic substitution: D2O/H2O substitution should alter first-shell ordering and exchange timescales beyond the mass-dependent isotope effect on diffusion (null hypothesis). Detection via chiral SFG spectroscopy (Perets et al., 2024) or nanomechanical measurement of water-exchange timescales in DNA films/cantilevers.

6.2 Counterion and temperature perturbations: Predicts systematic shifts in DNA first-shell observables under counterion substitution across the alkali series and under temperature scans. Observables tracking only ion charge and bulk viscosity (no network statistics dependence) would disfavor the mechanism. Motivated by Bi et al. (2026) showing weakly hydrated ions accelerate confined water transport in nanochannels.

6.3 Sequence dependence: AT-rich sequences (narrow minor grooves, coherent acceptor pattern) vs. GC-rich sequences (wider grooves, exocyclic amino group). Detection via chiral SFG or crystallographic water-occupancy comparisons.

6.4 Hydration and charge transport: Measure charge transport through matched and mismatched DNA (as in Slinker et al., 2011) and conductance vs. relative humidity (as in Tuukkanen et al., 2005) in H2O vs. D2O. Null hypothesis: mass-dependent isotope effect only. Signature: excess D2O effect on conduction or mismatch effect changing with hydration.

content_blocks.title: Section 7: Outlook
content_blocks.content: Proposes the mechanism, if confirmed at DNA, applies to other confined-water biological systems. References undocumented relationships between cellular water state, membrane potential, and tissue biomechanics (Cone, 1971; Holmes, 2026). Proposes a causal chain: molecule → shell → chromatin → cell. Notes potential oncological relevance: if the shell carries part of DNA's charge, damage disturbing the shell would show electrically.

content_blocks.title: Figure: DNA Hydration Shell Proposal — Argument Map
content_blocks.content: A flowchart-style argument map showing the logical structure of the paper's proposals. Four published-findings boxes at top: 'Hydration solids (Harrellson 2023)', 'Ordered DNA water (Perets 2024; Halle 1998)', 'Asymmetric H-bonds (Gunkel 2024)', 'Electrical H-bonds (Isaacs 1999; Slinker 2011)'. These feed into the central proposal: 'DNA minor groove as a hydration solid.' Three consequence branches: 'Ordering (Strong-weak matches sites)', 'Exchange (Extra re-randomization step)', 'Electrical pathway (Shell chains carry charge).' These lead to four proposed experiments (dashed boxes): 'D2O/H2O + SFG', 'Ions + temperature', 'AT vs GC grooves', 'Charge transport H2O vs D2O.' Final dashed box: 'Outlook: Cell water, chromatin, DNA damage.' Legend distinguishes published findings (solid boxes), this paper's proposals (solid boxes), and extensions (dashed boxes).

content_blocks.title: Section 8: Conclusion and References
content_blocks.content: Concludes that two established findings (hydration force governance of nanoscale biological lattices; intrinsic H-bond asymmetry in water) have developed without intersection, and proposes they meet in the DNA hydration shell. Proposes four experiments to test the mechanism. References include: Bakker/AMOLF (proton conduction); Bi et al. 2026 (Nature Communications, not yet confirmed); Cone 1971; Flór et al. 2024 (Science); Gunkel et al. 2024 (Nature Communications); Halle & Denisov 1998 (Biopolymers); Harrellson et al. 2023 (Nature); Holmes 2026 (Inventum Biologicum); Isaacs et al. 1999 (PRL); McDermott et al. 2017 (ACS Central Science); Perets & Yan 2017 (ACS Central Science); Perets et al. 2024 (J. Chem. Phys.); Santiago et al. 2025 (Chemical Science); Slinker et al. 2011 (Nature Chemistry, DOI unconfirmed); Tuukkanen et al. 2005 (Applied Physics Letters). Note: Bi et al. 2026 is cited as 'not yet confirmed' — a future/preprint reference.

key_findings: This is a purely theoretical/conceptual paper (TRL 1): no original experiments are reported; all empirical content is drawn from cited published literature.
Core proposal 1: The DNA minor groove qualifies as a 'hydration solid' under the Harrellson et al. (2023) framework, governed by the hydration force in its nanoscale channel geometry.

Core proposal 2: Intrinsic hydrogen bond asymmetry (Gunkel et al., 2024 — one strong, one weak bond per water molecule, anti-correlated, refreshed <500 fs) functions as a standing property of minor-groove spine water (~1 ns residence time), contributing to ordering and exchange dynamics.

Core proposal 3: The asymmetric hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway; DNA conductance drops ~40,000-fold from 80–90% to 30% relative humidity (Tuukkanen et al., 2005); a single base-pair mismatch halves charge transport signal (ratio 2.3 ± 0.4, Slinker et al., 2011).

Four experiments proposed (none performed): (1) D2O/H2O isotopic substitution + chiral SFG; (2) counterion/temperature perturbation of first-shell observables; (3) sequence-dependent (AT vs GC) shell comparison; (4) isotope-dependent DNA charge transport.
The Gunkel et al. (2024) asymmetry measurement was made in dimethylformamide, not pure water or biological context — a key limitation acknowledged by the author.
Author is affiliated with 'RIFOR,' a non-standard institutional affiliation; paper is self-described as a 'field synthesis' exercise, not a primary research report.
One cited reference (Bi et al., 2026) is explicitly flagged as 'not yet confirmed,' indicating the paper was written with awareness of very recent or preprint literature.
Broader outlook proposes causal chain from molecular water asymmetry to chromatin to cell, with potential oncological implications — highly speculative, no supporting data.
